meta.title: Canadian federal elections, 1867–2025
sources: Wikipedia election infoboxes and results tables for the 1st through 45th general elections (user-supplied extract, July 2026)

eras.label: Macdonald's Canada
eras.blurb: Seven elections in the young Dominion, six of them won by John A. Macdonald. The National Policy of protective tariffs, the transcontinental railway and the fight over Confederation itself defined the politics of a two-party country voting in stages, on open ballots until 1874.

eras.label: The Laurier era
eras.blurb: Wilfrid Laurier, the first francophone Prime Minister, won four straight majorities as the wheat boom filled the Prairies with new voters. It ended in 1911 over free trade with the United States, an argument Canada would resume 77 years later.

eras.label: War & fragmentation
eras.blurb: Conscription split the country on language lines in the khaki election of 1917, and the two-party system never fully recovered: the Progressives' 1921 revolt produced the first minority parliament, and the King–Byng affair turned the 1926 election into a constitutional referendum.

eras.label: The King–St. Laurent ascendancy
eras.blurb: Five consecutive Liberal majorities under Mackenzie King and Louis St. Laurent, spanning Depression, world war and the postwar boom, while the CCF and Social Credit turned Parliament into a four-party house.

eras.label: Diefenbaker & Pearson
eras.blurb: Five elections in eight years. John Diefenbaker's 1957 upset ended 22 Liberal years, his 1958 sweep set a record that stood for a generation, and then the pendulum jammed: four of the five contests produced minority governments.

eras.label: The Trudeau years
eras.blurb: Trudeaumania swept Pierre Trudeau to power in 1968; he governed for all but nine months of the next 16 years. The era closed with the West shut out of a Liberal government entirely, an alienation that would reshape the party system.

eras.label: Mulroney & the great collapse
eras.blurb: Brian Mulroney assembled the largest majority in Canadian history in 1984 and won the free-trade election of 1988, then his coalition shattered: in 1993 the Progressive Conservatives fell from government to two seats, the Bloc Québécois became the official opposition, and Jean Chrétien began a decade of Liberal majorities over a divided right.

eras.label: The modern battleground
eras.blurb: The merged Conservative Party made every election competitive again: seven minority parliaments out of nine contests, Stephen Harper's decade, Justin Trudeau's comeback and collapse, and in 2025 a two-party surge not seen since 1958, fought in the shadow of American tariffs.

elections.summary: The first election of the new Dominion, held over six weeks of open voting: Macdonald's Conservatives and their Liberal-Conservative allies won comfortably, though Joseph Howe's Anti-Confederates took 18 of Nova Scotia's 19 seats on a platform of leaving Canada.

Macdonald hung on with a bare working majority against Blake and Mackenzie's Liberals, the campaign financed by railway promoter Hugh Allan's money, the seed of the Pacific Scandal that destroyed the government within a year.
Alexander Mackenzie's Liberals, in office three months after the Pacific Scandal toppled Macdonald, won a decisive mandate in the first election held on a single day with secret ballots.
Macdonald completed his comeback from the Pacific Scandal, sweeping back to power on the National Policy of protective tariffs against Mackenzie's depression-worn free-trade government.
Macdonald's third majority, the National Policy tariffs in full operation and the Canadian Pacific Railway under construction.
Macdonald won a fourth term over new Liberal leader Edward Blake, weathering Quebec's fury at the hanging of Louis Riel and provincial-rights revolts in Ontario and Nova Scotia.

elections.knownAs: The old flag, the old policy
elections.summary: 'The old flag, the old policy, the old leader': Macdonald's last campaign, fought against Liberal 'unrestricted reciprocity' with the loyalty cry, won him a fifth majority. He died three months later.

Wilfrid Laurier became the first French-Canadian Prime Minister, winning on the Manitoba Schools Question despite taking fewer votes than Tupper's Conservatives, and settling it by compromise ('sunny ways'). The Liberals would govern for fifteen years.
Laurier consolidated his majority as the Boer War strained his balancing act between imperial sentiment in Ontario and opposition in Quebec, sweeping his home province.
Laurier won a third majority on the wheat boom and his promise of a second transcontinental railway, the Grand Trunk Pacific.
'Let Laurier finish his work': a fourth consecutive Liberal majority, reduced but comfortable, over Borden's Conservatives campaigning against corruption.

The reciprocity election: Laurier's free-trade agreement with the United States united Ontario manufacturers and imperial loyalists against him ('No truck nor trade with the Yankees'), while Henri Bourassa's nationalistes attacked his naval policy in Quebec. Borden's Conservatives ended fifteen years of Liberal rule.

The khaki election, the bitterest in Canadian history: Borden's Union government of Conservatives and conscriptionist Liberals crushed Laurier's rump on the conscription question, winning three seats in Quebec against 62. The Wartime Elections Act gave votes to soldiers' female relatives while stripping them from 'enemy-alien' naturalized citizens.

The party system shattered: Agnes Macphail became the first woman MP as the farmers' Progressive movement took 58 seats, more than the Conservatives, and Mackenzie King began his 27-year dominance with the first minority Parliament in Canadian history.

Arthur Meighen's Conservatives won the most seats, 115 to 100, but Mackenzie King refused to resign, governing with Progressive support despite having lost his own seat. The arrangement collapsed within a year into the King–Byng affair.

The King–Byng election: after Governor General Byng refused King a dissolution and Meighen's three-day government fell, King campaigned against imperial interference and returned with 116 seats and effective control, an episode still cited in every constitutional crisis since.
R.B. Bennett's Conservatives won a majority as the Depression began, promising to 'blast a way' into world markets with tariffs. Five years of catastrophe followed, and King inherited the recovery.

'King or Chaos': the Liberals crushed R.B. Bennett's Depression-battered Conservatives with 173 seats on just 44.7% of the vote, as the new CCF and Social Credit parties and Bennett's renegade Reconstruction Party splintered the opposition.

King sought and won a wartime mandate with 179 seats, the largest majority to that date, after Ontario Premier Mitchell Hepburn's condemnation of his war effort handed him the pretext for dissolution.

Mackenzie King narrowly survived the war he had managed, winning 118 seats days after V-E Day despite losing his own riding, while the CCF's 28 seats marked the socialist high-water mark that had panicked both old parties into embracing the welfare state.
St. Laurent's first election as leader delivered 191 seats, then the largest caucus in Canadian history, with Newfoundland voting federally for the first time after joining Confederation that spring.
Louis St. Laurent cruised to a second majority, 'Uncle Louis' presiding over postwar prosperity against George Drew's Conservatives.

John Diefenbaker's Progressive Conservatives ended 22 consecutive years of Liberal government with a minority upset over St. Laurent, whose party had won the popular vote. Within a year Diefenbaker would convert it into the biggest landslide in Canadian history.

The Diefenbaker sweep: 208 of 265 seats, still the largest share of the House ever won, including 50 of Quebec's 75 as Union Nationale machinery swung behind him. 'Follow John' carried every province.
Diefenbaker's 208-seat colossus shrank to a minority of 116 as Social Credit's créditiste wing took 26 seats in Quebec under Réal Caouette and the economy soured with the devalued 'Diefenbuck'.

The collapse of Diefenbaker's government over nuclear warheads for Bomarc missiles let Lester Pearson form a minority government, beginning the five-year Parliament that produced medicare, the pension plan and the flag.

Pearson called an early election seeking a majority and missed it by two seats, prompting Tommy Douglas's quip that the country had spent sixty million dollars to buy the same Parliament. It was Diefenbaker's last campaign as leader.

Trudeaumania: three weeks after winning the Liberal leadership, Pierre Trudeau won the majority that had eluded Pearson, campaigning for a 'Just Society' against a Conservative Party still led by the man he would dominate, Robert Stanfield.
Trudeau clung to power by two seats, 109 to Stanfield's 107, the closest result in federal history, governing for two years with NDP support under David Lewis's 'corporate welfare bums' Parliament.
Trudeau regained his majority by campaigning against Robert Stanfield's proposed wage and price controls ('Zap, you're frozen'), then imposed controls himself the following year.

Joe Clark became, at 39, the youngest Prime Minister in Canadian history, his 136 seats short of a majority. Trudeau's Liberals won the popular vote by four points but piled up wasted majorities in Quebec.

Joe Clark's government fell on its first budget after nine months, and Pierre Trudeau, who had announced his retirement weeks earlier, returned with a majority. The Liberals won nothing west of Manitoba, and Trudeau's National Energy Program would deepen the alienation.

Brian Mulroney's 211 seats remain the most ever won by a Canadian party, a sweep of every province including 58 of Quebec's 75 seats, ending two decades of Liberal dominance. John Turner had been Prime Minister for 79 days.

The free trade election: John Turner vowed to tear up the Canada–US Free Trade Agreement and Brian Mulroney staked his government on it. Mulroney's 169 seats ratified the deal, though a majority of voters backed parties opposed to it.

The most dramatic result in Canadian history: Kim Campbell's Progressive Conservatives fell from 156 seats to 2, the Bloc Québécois became official opposition in its first election, Reform swept the West, and Jean Chrétien's Liberals took a majority of 177.
Chrétien held his majority with 155 seats in a five-party House: Preston Manning's Reform became official opposition, the Bloc slipped, and the PCs and NDP recovered official party status.
Jean Chrétien called an early election against the new Canadian Alliance and won a third straight majority with 172 seats, Stockwell Day's breakthrough failing to materialize east of Manitoba.

Paul Martin, freshly installed as Prime Minister, was reduced to a minority as the sponsorship scandal broke and the newly merged Conservative Party under Harper fought its first campaign, ending the era of the divided right.
Stephen Harper's Conservatives ended twelve years of Liberal rule with a minority of 124 seats, the sponsorship scandal having done for Paul Martin's government within two years of his taking office.
Harper's gamble on an early election strengthened his minority to 143 seats against Stéphane Dion's Liberals, on the lowest turnout in Canadian federal history, 58.8%.

Stephen Harper finally won his majority while Jack Layton's NDP surged to 103 seats and official opposition for the first time, the 'orange wave' sweeping Quebec. The Liberals fell to third with their worst result ever, and the Bloc was reduced to four seats.
Justin Trudeau took the Liberals from third place and 36 seats to a 184-seat majority, the largest seat gain in Canadian history, ending Stephen Harper's decade in the longest campaign since 1872.

Trudeau lost his majority and the popular vote but kept power, taking 157 seats to Andrew Scheer's 121. The Bloc Québécois tripled its caucus and the divide between a Liberal east and Conservative west sharpened.

Justin Trudeau's pandemic snap election returned an almost identical Parliament to the one he dissolved: a Liberal minority of 160 on the lowest turnout since 2008, with the Conservatives under Erin O'Toole again winning the popular vote.

Mark Carney, Prime Minister for barely six weeks, led the Liberals to a fourth consecutive term in an election dominated by Donald Trump's tariffs and talk of annexation. The Liberals and Conservatives together took over 85% of the vote, the highest two-party share since 1958; Conservative leader Pierre Poilievre lost his own Ottawa-area seat even as his party gained ground.
